# tshark-mcp

> Read-only MCP server that lets an agent analyse existing packet captures with tshark. Twenty-three tools return compact JSON for Diameter, GTPv2-C, GTPv1-C, GTP-U, SIP, RTP/RTCP, SCTP/M3UA/SCCP/TCAP/MAP, DNS and TLS handshakes, pair requests with answers, name result codes and flag what never got a reply, and say whether the capture itself can be trusted for loss conclusions. It cannot capture, write, export, resolve names or load code.

## What it can and cannot do

- Reads capture files that already exist inside directories the operator allowed with `--allow-dir`. Every path an agent passes must resolve (symlinks followed) inside one of them; anything else is refused before the file is looked at.
- Every call is bounded: file size (500 MB), matching packets dissected in full (500 per call), frames read per tshark run (200 000), JSON returned (30 KB by default, about 8k tokens; rows past it go to the next page), tshark run time (60 s), files opened by one multi-file call (50).
- tshark is started with an argv list, never a shell, always with `-n` (no name resolution) and `-r` (read a file). Capture, write, export and extension flags are refused before a process starts; `-o` is allowed only for the three checksum-validation preferences the server sets itself.
- Display filters are linted and compiled against an empty capture before touching the real file. Field names must exist in `tshark -G fields`.
- Failures come back as `{"error": {"type": ..., "message": ...}}`, never as exceptions.
- Every tool with a `limit` also takes `offset` (in `find_identifier` it skips files of the directory).
- A capture that ends mid-packet is read up to the damage; the result then carries `warnings`.
- Every call is written to a JSON-lines audit log when `--log-file` is set.
- Supported transport: stdio. `--transport streamable-http` exists for local experiments only and has no authentication.

## Tools

- `find_identifier(path, identifier, kind="auto", max_files=20, offset=0)`: which files in a directory mention an IMSI, MSISDN, IP address, SIP Call-ID or Diameter Session-Id; hit counts, first/last timestamps, protocol breakdown per file. Call this first when you do not know which capture to open.
- `pcap_info(path)`: packet count, duration, first/last timestamp, link type, protocol hierarchy, active limits. Call this first on a file.
- `capture_quality(path)`: can missing packets and retransmissions in this file be read as network faults? Duplicate copies of the same packet and their cause, TCP bytes the receiver acknowledged that the capture never saw (the capture dropped them), gaps a retransmission filled (lost before the capture point), snaplen-truncated frames, segmentation-offload packets above 1500 bytes, bad checksums and whether they are offload artifacts, one-direction TCP streams, backwards or coarse timestamps; `verdict.loss_conclusions` is trustworthy, use with care or not trustworthy, with reasons. Call it before blaming the network for loss.
- `tcp_health(path, filter=None, stream=None, mtu=1500, limit=100, offset=0)`: per TCP stream with mirror/SPAN copies dropped: handshake RTT split at the capture point, MSS, window scale; retransmissions by where the loss happened (before the capture point, after it, or only missing from the capture), reordering, duplicate ACKs, zero windows; who sent each reset (endpoint or a middlebox, by TTL and MAC) and the idle time before it; ICMP errors about the stream; MSS too large for `mtu` and the PMTUD black-hole pattern. Use it instead of tshark's tcp.analysis flags, which count copies as retransmissions.
- `conversations(path, layer="ip", filter=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: top talkers at ip, ipv6, tcp, udp, sctp or eth, optionally restricted by a display filter.
- `filter_packets(path, display_filter, fields=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: rows of fields for packets matching a display filter; the escape hatch for anything the protocol tools do not cover.
- `diameter_sessions(path, session_id=None, imsi=None, command_code=None, filter=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: Diameter grouped by Session-Id with the paired transactions, result codes, unanswered and failed counts.
- `diameter_transactions(path, filter=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: every Diameter request paired with its answer by Hop-by-Hop and End-to-End id within its Session-Id; command, hosts, User-Name, Result-Code or Experimental-Result-Code with its name, RTT, `unanswered`.
- `diameter_avps(path, session_id=None, imsi=None, command_code=None, frame=None, filter=None, detail="key", max_avps=200, limit=20, offset=0)`: the AVPs of paired Diameter transactions. `key` gives result codes, procedure flags with bit names (ULR, CLR, PUR, PUA, IDR, ...), Cancellation-Type, RAT-Type, Gx request type and rule reports, and a Subscription-Data digest with one line per APN; `full` gives the whole AVP tree, capped per message. Use it when a transaction row needs the why (what the HSS sent, why the MME asked).
- `gtp_sessions(path, imsi=None, apn=None, teid=None, filter=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: GTPv2-C requests paired with responses by sequence number; IMSI, APN, F-TEIDs, cause, PAA. On captures with several proxy legs of one procedure, a leg without a response while another leg was answered is `leg_without_response` with a `note` (response not relayed back, or the proxy answered on its own), not `unanswered`; a packet captured twice is `duplicate_of_frame`.
- `gtpv1_sessions(path, imsi=None, apn=None, teid=None, filter=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: GTPv1-C (Gn/Gp) PDP context signalling paired by sequence number, with APN, NSAPI, TEIDs, GSN addresses, end-user address and cause names; same proxy-chain fields as gtp_sessions.
- `gtp_user_plane(path, teid=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: GTP-U packets and bytes per tunnel endpoint id with inner addresses.
- `gtp_tunnel_health(path, teid=None, mtu=1500, limit=200, offset=0)`: user-plane health per GTP-U tunnel: inner TCP retransmissions, reordering, resets and the MSS in SYNs against the tunnel overhead and path MTU, inner and outer ICMP errors (fragmentation needed), one-way tunnels, all summed up in `issues`. Use it for slow or stalled data sessions instead of raw tshark; it ignores duplicate copies of packets, which tshark's own analysis counts as retransmissions.
- `message_rates(path, protocol="auto", interval=1.0, imsi=None, filter=None, burst_min=5, storm_min=5, limit=50, offset=0)`: messages per second (or per `interval`) by name, bursts against the usual rate, and subscribers looping on one request (purge, attach or registration storms) with the gap between repeats. Relayed and retransmitted copies count once. Protocols: diameter, gtpv2, gtpv1, sip, map; MAP messages take the IMSI named anywhere in their TCAP dialogue, GTP responses the IMSI of their request.
- `dns_transactions(path, name=None, filter=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: DNS queries paired with responses, unanswered queries included (which tshark's dns.time cannot show): rcode names, RTT, resends and retries, TC answers and TCP fallback, per-server latency percentiles and unanswered share, the failing names, `issues`. `name` matches the name and its subdomains. Use it for "cannot resolve", slow resolvers and SERVFAIL/NXDOMAIN questions, including DNS inside GTP-U tunnels.
- `tls_handshakes(path, server_name=None, filter=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: per TLS (TCP) or QUIC connection, the ClientHello offer against the ServerHello choice, alerts and who sent them, the certificate (TLS 1.2 and older), and an `outcome` with a plain-words `note`; `issues` flags expired certificates, SNI not covered by the certificate, deprecated versions and HelloRetryRequest. No decryption. Use it for "TLS handshake failed", "certificate error" and "which app servers did the UE fail to reach"; `server_name` matches the SNI and its subdomains.
- `sip_dialogs(path, call_id=None, number=None, method=None, filter=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: SIP grouped by Call-ID with the method chain, From/To, final status, time to final response and duration; several messages in one TCP segment are each counted in their own dialog.
- `sip_call_detail(path, call_id)`: one call in detail: post-dial delay, answer and setup times, call duration, retransmissions, final response, Reason (Q.850 named) and Warning headers, who hung up, and the SDP offer/answer with the codecs both sides share (empty after a 488 means a codec mismatch). Use it after `sip_dialogs` finds the Call-ID.
- `rtp_streams(path, call_id=None, ssrc=None, heuristic=False, filter=None, limit=100, offset=0)`: RTP streams per SSRC linked to the SIP Call-ID through the SDP addresses and ports, with codec, packets, loss, sequence errors, jitter, deltas, duration, the reverse stream or `one_way`, RTCP reports (loss, jitter, round trip) and a `mos_estimate`. The MOS is a simplified G.107 E-model estimate from network metrics, returned with its method and inputs; never present it as a measured MOS. Set `heuristic=true` when the capture has RTP but not the SIP/SDP.
- `sctp_associations(path, limit=200, offset=0)`: SCTP handshake state, heartbeats, retransmissions, aborts per endpoint pair.
- `sigtran_messages(path, filter=None, limit=200, offset=0)`: M3UA/SCCP/TCAP/MAP messages with global titles, operation names, IMSI and MSISDN.
- `compare_captures(path_a, path_b, imsi=None, msisdn=None, imsi_b=None, msisdn_b=None, collapse_repeats=True, limit=100, offset=0)`: a working and a failing capture of the same procedure: aligned message ladders, the first divergence, the AVP/IE differences of each changed step and the timing gaps. Give `imsi_b` when the failing capture is another subscriber; with no identity every transaction is compared.
- `trace_subscriber(path, imsi=None, msisdn=None, limit=300, offset=0)`: one time-ordered timeline for a subscriber across Diameter, GTPv2-C, GTPv1-C, MAP and SIP; all its passes share one time budget. Start here for "why did subscriber X fail".

## How to work with it

1. `find_identifier` on the directory, then `pcap_info` on the file it points at; `capture_quality` before drawing loss or timing conclusions from it.
2. `trace_subscriber` for the subscriber (or `compare_captures` when a working capture exists too), then the protocol tool whose row needs more detail, using the structured filters (`imsi`, `session_id`, `call_id`, `teid`, `apn`, `method`) before raw display filters.
3. List tools return one page: `total_matched`, `returned`, `dropped` after the page, and `next_offset` when more rows exist. Call again with `offset=next_offset` and the same arguments for the next page. `truncated: true` always comes with a `truncated_reason` saying how to get the rest; `total_is_lower_bound: true` means a packet or frame cap stopped the scan, so narrow the filter instead of paging. Never conclude something is absent from a truncated result.
4. Pairing follows what is in the file. A request whose answer was captured elsewhere is reported as `unanswered`.
